paper_title: Self-Supervised Dataset Distillation via Mutual Information Maximization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Dataset distillation (DD) aims to compress a large dataset into a small synthetic one that remains effective for training neural networks. Despite its success in supervised learning, DD remains underexplored in self-supervised learning (SSL), where distilled data must preserve the information needed to learn representations that remain consistent across augmentations. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mutual Information Prototype Alignment (MIPA), an efficient SSL dataset distillation approach that optimizes synthetic images to preserve augmentation-invariant information. Specifically, MIPA treats synthetic images as learnable prototypes and uses a frozen encoder to assign real samples to them based on feature similarity. A synthetic dataset that preserves such augmentation invariance should yield stable prototype assignments across multiple augmented views of the same real image. MIPA encourages this by maximizing mutual information between cross-view assignments while avoiding trivial solutions in which all real samples are assigned to only a few synthetic prototypes. Evaluations on image classification benchmarks show that synthetic data generated by MIPA yield higher-quality representations than existing distillation approaches while reducing time and storage demands during distillation.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Dataset distillation (DD) aims to compress large dataset into small synthetic one that remains effective for training neural networks. Despite its success in supervised learning, DD remains underexplored in self-supervised learning (SSL), where distilled data must preserve the information needed to learn representations that remain consistent across augmentations. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mutual Information Prototype Alignment (MIPA), an efficient SSL dataset distillation approach that optimizes synthetic images to preserve augmentation-invariant information. Specifically, MIPA treats synthetic images as learnable prototypes and uses frozen encoder to assign real samples to them based on feature similarity. synthetic dataset that preserves such augmentation invariance should yield stable prototype assignments across multiple augmented views of the same real image. MIPA encourages this by maximizing mutual information between cross-view assignments while avoiding trivial solutions in which all real samples are assigned to only few synthetic prototypes. Evaluations on image classification benchmarks show that synthetic data generated by MIPA yield higher-quality representations than existing distillation approaches while reducing time and storage demands during distillation. Code is available at https://github.com/mhmoslemi/MIPA.git 1. Introduction Dataset distillation (DD) seeks to condense large dataset into compact set of synthetic samples that approximate the effect of training on the full dataset while reducing memory and computational requirements [29]. This makes DD attractive for edge model training and continual learning, while its privacy implications have also received attention [3, 8, 27, 36]. However, most existing DD methods focus on supervised settings that assume access to class labels, which are often scarce or unavailable in practice. In such cases, self-supervised learning (SSL) offers an alternative by pretraining an encoder on large amounts of unlabeled data, which can subsequently be adapted to range of downstream tasks. Accordingly, the computational and memory advantages of DD could also benefit SSL. Despite this potential, SSL-DD remains relatively underexplored. compact synthetic dataset for SSL must preserve sufficient augmentation-invariant information from the original large-scale one to support learning useful representations with SSL. Existing supervised DD methods, including gradient matching [33, 35], distribution matching [34], and trajectory matching [3], are not effective in this setting as their objectives rely on class-label supervision rather than the specific requirements of SSL. More recently, KRR-ST [20] and MKDT [16] have attempted to bridge this gap by adapting supervised DD techniques using auxiliary target representations as supervision signals without fully accounting for the distinct learning objectives of SSL. Consequently, both methods require auxiliary target representations alongside the synthetic images during SSL pretraining. This dependence undermines the goal of standalone DD by increasing storage overhead, requiring target-matching losses instead of standard SSL objectives, and introducing potential security vulnerabilities associated with malicious teacher representations [5]. Notably, we observe that removing these auxiliary representations and pretraining only on synthetic images does not reliably outperform randomly selecting real samples from the original dataset. In this work, rather than adapting supervised DD to SSL, we design an approach that directly accounts for the augmentation-invariance requirement of SSL. To this end, we introduce Mutual Information Prototype Alignment (MIPA), which treats synthetic images as learnable prototypes in the representation space. In particular, for each real image, MIPA computes probability distribution over these prototypes based on feature similarity, indicating the degree 1 to which each synthetic image matches the real sample. It then evaluates these assignments over multiple views of the same image. Preserving augmentation-invariant information in synthetic data should yield consistent assignments for different views of the same real image. Simply minimizing distance-based objectives between assignments can result in trivial solutions in which all real images are assigned to the same limited subset of synthetic prototypes. Instead, MIPA maximizes mutual information between cross-view assignments by optimizing the synthetic data, promoting consistency in assignments while avoiding such collapse, as demonstrated by our analysis and empirical results. Figure 1a illustrates this procedure by showing assignment distributions from two views of the same real image. (a) (b) Figure 1. Assignment distributions and efficiency comparison. Figure 1a shows two augmented views of the same real image (left) mapped to shared synthetic prototypes (middle); the top and mirrored bottom bars indicate the assignment distributions. Figure 1b compares Prior (MKDT [16]) and Ours (MIPA) on CIFAR10 with synthetic set of 0.2% of the training data. We pretrain ResNet-18 from scratch with SimCLR on synthetic images only, followed by linear classifier with 1% labeled data. We evaluate MIPA on image classification benchmarks across multiple architectures and SSL methods. Our results indicate that MIPA yields higher-quality representations than prior distillation and sample selection approaches. More importantly, as shown in Figure 1b, MIPA achieves higher accuracy while significantly reducing the time and storage required during distillation. In particular, we make the following contributions: 1. We identify augmentation consistency and prototype diversity as key to SSL distillation, demonstrating that consistency alone can lead to trivial solutions. 2. We propose MIPA, which maximizes mutual information between cross-view prototype assignments to enable SSL pretraining from scratch using only synthetic data. 3. Comprehensive experiments confirm MIPAs effectiveness on downstream tasks while substantially reducing distillation time and storage requirements. 2. Related Work 2.1. Dataset Distillation Dataset distillation was first formulated as bilevel optimization problem [29]. Subsequent approaches include 2 gradient matching [35], distribution matching [34], kernelbased meta-learning [26], and training trajectory matching [3, 9]. Recent work further incorporates optimal transport into distribution-matching objectives [22]. Complementary studies investigate adversarial attacks [30], privacy [36], fairness [25], and robustness to domain shifts [23, 28]. Most of these methods operate in supervised settings. Other approaches leverage pretrained SSL encoders for data distillation under different assumptions. SC-DD [37] reconstructs images using batch-normalization statistics with class supervision, while LGM [4] learns labeled synthetic data by matching linear-classifier gradients on frozen SSL features. SRG [21] further utilizes class prototypes in SSL representation space to guide diffusion-based synthesis. Self-supervised dataset distillation instead seeks to compress data without any class labels. KRR-ST [20] adapts kernel-based matching to this setting. However, MKDT [16] reported that KRR-ST did not consistently outperform SSL pretraining on random real subsets and further showed that MTT [3], although label-agnostic in principle, performs poorly when applied to SSL. MKDT instead replaces high-variance SSL trajectories with lowervariance knowledge-distillation trajectories. Yu et al. [31] further investigate SSL distillation by jointly optimizing synthetic images and target representations, using predefined augmentations and an approximation network to mitigate augmentation-related instability. Similar to KRR-ST and MKDT, this approach retains auxiliary representation targets for subsequent training. In contrast, MIPA uses frozen SSL encoder solely to guide distillation, avoids inner-loop encoder training, and produces synthetic images that independently support SSL pretraining from scratch without class labels or auxiliary target representations. 2.2. Self-Supervised Learning Self-supervised learning aims to learn transferable representations from unlabeled data. Contrastive methods such as SimCLR [6] and MoCo [12] align augmented views of the same image while separating representations of different images. BYOL [10] and SimSiam [7] learn through prediction between views without explicit negative pairs. Barlow Twins [32] regularizes representation statistics by encouraging the cross-correlation matrix computed between two views toward the identity matrix. Clustering-based methods such as SwAV [2] instead assign representations of augmented views to learnable prototypes and enforce consistency between their assignments across views. Masked prediction techniques learn from partially observed inputs. For example, MAE [13] masks random patches of the input image and trains an encoder-decoder architecture to reconstruct the missing pixels. In contrast, I-JEPA [1] predicts the representations of target regions from context region of the same image directly in feature space. We compare against three sample selection methods, RANDOM, K-MEANS, and SAS [15], as well as two SSL-DD methods KRR-ST [20] and MKDT [16]. RANDOM selects real training images uniformly at random, whereas K-MEANS performs clustering over pretrained encoder embeddings of the full training set and then chooses real images closest to the resulting centroids. SAS also selects real samples based on their expected similarity to augmented views of other training examples, prioritizing those that are most beneficial for contrastive SSL. For KRR-ST and MKDT, we generate distilled sets using their official implementations. For consistent image-only comparison, we evaluate KRR-ST and MKDT using their synthetic images alone, excluding the auxiliary target representations required by their original procedures. This evaluates the standalone utility of the distilled images under common from-scratch SSL protocol, rather than the performance of their complete training pipelines. We focus on this setting because the resulting datasets can be reused with standard SSL objectives without method-specific auxiliary targets. Methods that train classifier on top of frozen pretrained encoder (e.g., [4, 37]) address different downstream setting and are not directly comparable here. We also report SSL results using the full training set as an upper-bound reference. Distillation setup. We first pretrain ResNet-18 [11] encoder with BatchNorm on the full unlabeled training set using SimCLR [6] for 1k epochs and keep it frozen for the whole distillation process. Prototype assignments are then obtained from cosine similarities between embeddings produced by this frozen teacher from augmented views of real and synthetic images using temperature τ of 0.2. Unless otherwise noted, synthetic data are initialized by randomly sampling real images from the full dataset, and then optimized with Adam using learning rate of 0.001 and batch size of 128. We consider synthetic dataset sizes of 0.2%, 1%, and 2% of the full training set and run MIPA for 10k, 8k, and 6k iterations, respectively. Evaluation setup. For each method and dataset budget, we train ResNet-18 encoder from scratch using SimCLR on the resulting images alone. For KRR-ST and MKDT, this excludes the additional target representations required by their original downstream SSL procedures. We assess classification on the source dataset and transfer to downstream tasks through linear probing. In each case, we freeze the encoder and train linear probe using either 1% or 5% from the labeled training data of the evaluation dataset, then measure accuracy on its test set. We repeat each evaluation over five independent runs and report the mean accuracy. 5.2. Results and Discussion Main results. Table 1 shows that MIPA achieves the highest mean accuracy among reduced-data methods across all reported configurations, although some improvements over the strongest baselines are small relative to the reported variability. Its improvements over the sample selection baselines suggest the benefit of optimizing synthetic images rather than selecting real samples. The gains are consistent on CIFAR-10 and become more pronounced on CIFAR-100 as the synthetic set size increases. At the 2% CIFAR-100 setting, MIPA exceeds the strongest baseline, SAS, by 3.14 and 2.90 percentage points with 1% and 5% labeled data, respectively. Gains on Tiny ImageNet are smaller but remain consistent across the evaluated settings. MIPA also consistently benefits from larger synthetic datasets, whereas MKDT shows only marginal improvements or even declines in accuracy as the dataset size increases. One possible explanation is that MKDT optimizes synthetic images to be used alongside teacher-derived representations, so increasing the synthetic budget does not necessarily improve their standalone utility when these targets are removed. Both KRR-ST and MKDT generally underperform RANDOM under our image-only evaluation protocol, with KRR-ST showing particularly large performance gaps on CIFAR-10. Importantly, both methods originally rely on auxiliary target representations alongside synthetic images for pretraining. Overall, MIPA outperforms these methods using only synthetic images for SSL pretraining from scratch, although gap to full-data pretraining still remains. Cross-dataset generalization. In this section, we evaluate how well models trained on synthetic datasets distilled by MIPA generalize when the downstream evaluation dataset differs from that used for SSL pretraining. Figure 3 illustrates the results. As shown in the figure, MIPA matches or outperforms the other evaluated methods in every transfer setting among CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet across different configurations. Increasing the synthetic set size also consistently improves MIPAs downstream accuracy across all evaluated settings, indicating that the advantages of larger distilled set generalize beyond classification on the source dataset. Transfer to Aircraft and Dogs, however, is less stable, as MKDT or RANDOM can outperform MIPA in some settings. Overall, these results indicate that MIPA continues to perform well in downstream evaluations, although performance gaps between methods are often relatively minor. Cross-architecture generalization. We evaluate whether the gains of MIPA persist when pretraining deeper networks than the one used to generate synthetic data. We use ResNet-18 as the frozen encoder during distillation and the resulting synthetic data to pretrain ResNet-34 and ResNet-50 encoders. Table 2 reports the results. MIPA outperforms RANDOM on the source dataset in every evaluated setting, showing its gains extend to encoders different from the one used during distillation. Downstream accuracy also improves across all ResNet-50 and most ResNet34 settings. With ResNet-34, the larger CIFAR-10 synthetic set yields higher source-dataset accuracy but slightly lower downstream accuracy on CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet. MIPA also performs slightly worse than RANDOM when transferring from the smaller CIFAR-100 synthetic data to CIFAR-10. Overall, MIPA maintains its benefits across architectures, with few exceptions in downstream tasks. Figure 4. Figure 4 shows that MIPA outperforms RANDOM in all evaluated settings. However, increasing batch size does not necessarily improve performance. This may occur because averaging the joint assignment matrix over large batches smooths the empirical marginal distribution, weakening gradient signals from the marginal entropy term HP (C1) that encourages diverse prototype usage. Turning to the assignment temperature, the sweep shows that an intermediate value of τ = 0.2 performs best. Smaller temperatures produce overly sharp assignments, while larger temperatures make assignments more uniform across synthetic images. An intermediate temperature may therefore preserve distinctions between real images while avoiding excessive concentration on individual prototypes. Ablation on the distillation objective. In Section 4.1, we explained that naively enforcing assignment agreement between augmented views can lead to collapse and trivial solutions. Here, we empirically verify this behavior. Specifically, we perform distillation using the agreement objective Lagree from Eq. (7) and compare it with RANDOM and MIPA. Table 3 summarizes the results, indicating that optimizing Lagree alone causes collapse and yields performance worse than RANDOM. This finding is consistent with our analysis and supports the use of mutual information to promote diverse prototype assignments while maintaining agreement between augmented views. Table 3. Next, we evaluate whether the benefits of MIPA generalize to an SSL method beyond SimCLR. Specifically, we pretrain an encoder from scratch using Barlow Twins on synthetic data produced by MIPA, where the frozen teacher was trained with SimCLR. Table 4 presents the results, indicating that MIPA consistently surpasses RANDOM on the source dataset across all settings and in every downstream evaluation except one. It also consistently outperforms MKDT. These results indicate that images distilled using teacher trained with SimCLR remain effective for pretraining with Barlow Twins. Effect of initialization. We investigate how the initialization of synthetic images affects MIPA. We compare randomly selected real images, K-means, Invariant Information Clustering (IIC) [14], and Gaussian noise. Since optimization from noise may require more iterations to converge, we also evaluate Gaussian initialization with 3 and 10 the default distillation iterations. Table 5 presents the results. Random real-image initialization achieves the highest mean accuracy across all settings, with neither clustering method providing an advantage. One possible explanation is that clustering prioritizes representative samples based on feature-space structure, which may not necessarily align with the augmentation-invariant information targeted by MIPA. In contrast, random sampling provides diverse real-image structures without introducing clustering bias. Gaussian noise initialization performs substantially worse, even with 10 more iterations. Although additional iterations partially improve performance, the gains are small and inconsistent, and accuracy remains below all real-imagebased initializations. These findings suggest that real images provide useful initial structure that is difficult to recover from noise, while random sampling offers an effective initialization without additional clustering overhead. All runtimes were measured on single NVIDIA L40S GPU. These measurements quantify distillation overhead rather than total end-to-end training cost. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, MIPA is approximately 5.88.0 faster than MKDT, even before accounting for the additional cost of generating MKDTs expert trajectories. On Tiny ImageNet, MIPA remains faster, although the speedup decreases as the synthetic dataset size increases. Furthermore, by eliminating the need for expert trajectory buffers, MIPA reduces intermediate disk storage by more than 250 across all three datasets, substantially lowering the resources required for distillation. Bottom: independent Gaussian-noise-initialized prototypes at the 0.2% data budget after 50k iterations. 6. Conclusion Prototype visualization. Figure 5 illustrates the synthetic images generated by MIPA using real-image initialization, alongside examples initialized from Gaussian noise. With real-image initialization, the optimized CIFAR-100 prototypes largely preserve the original object structures while showing noticeable changes in color, contrast, and texture. Some examples exhibit more distinct boundaries, while others develop visible distortions, indicating that MIPA modifies the original images during distillation. In contrast, the Gaussian-noise-initialized prototypes exhibit geometric patterns and local textures but little recognizable object structure. In this work, we introduced MIPA, self-supervised dataset distillation method that enables SSL pretraining from scratch using only synthetic images, without requiring auxiliary target representations during SSL pretraining. By maximizing mutual information between crossview prototype assignments, MIPA produces compact synthetic datasets that outperform the evaluated image-only baselines while substantially reducing distillation time and storage requirements. Extensive evaluations on image classification and various downstream tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of MIPA across different model architectures, SSL methods, and synthetic dataset sizes.
